title: Staying Connected with Grown Children
description: For parents of young adults and adult children. The relationship changes from guiding to supporting: these routines keep you close while respecting that they run their own lives, including when they're going through a hard time.

routines.title: A Regular Catch-Up
routines.description: A standing call, walk or meal at a time that suits them, so staying in touch doesn't depend on a problem.
routines.parentGoal: Keep a steady, low-pressure line of connection.
routines.childOutcome: Knows you're there without feeling checked on.
steps: Agree together on a time and a way that suits them: a call, a walk, a meal.
Start with their news and listen more than you talk.
Keep it short and light; end before it feels like an obligation.

routines.title: Ask for Their Advice
routines.description: Ask their opinion on something they know about, the way you would with any adult you respect.
routines.parentGoal: Show that you see them as a capable adult.
routines.childOutcome: Feels respected and trusted, which makes them more open in return.
steps: Pick something they know well: a skill, a topic, a decision you're weighing.
Ask a real question and take the answer seriously.
Say what you found useful about it.

routines.title: Listen Before Helping
routines.description: When they bring you a problem, ask what kind of support they want before offering any.
routines.childOutcome: Keeps ownership of their decisions and comes back to you more often.
steps: Ask: "Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?"
Do what they ask, even if you have a good idea.
If you do give advice, offer it once and let it go.

routines.title: Reach Out After a Disagreement
routines.description: After a tense conversation, send a short, warm message that keeps the door open without reopening the argument.
routines.parentGoal: Repair the relationship without needing to win the point.
routines.childOutcome: Learns that disagreements don't threaten the relationship.
steps: Wait until you're calm, then write a short message.
Say something like: "I didn't like how that went. I love you, and I'm here when you want to talk."
Don't restate your argument or ask for a reply.

routines.title: Name Your Limits Kindly
routines.description: Say clearly and calmly what you can and can't do (money, time, help at home) instead of giving in or arguing.
routines.parentGoal: Hold your own boundaries while staying warm.
routines.childOutcome: Knows where they stand, which builds their independence.
steps: Decide beforehand what you're comfortable offering.
Say it simply: "I can help with this, but not with that."
Stay kind and brief; you don't need to justify it at length.

routines.title: Say What You've Noticed, Gently
routines.description: When something seems off, share one specific thing you've noticed and invite them to talk, without labels or alarm.
routines.parentGoal: Open a conversation about how they're doing without making them defensive.
routines.childOutcome: Feels noticed and cared about, and knows they can talk when ready.
steps: Pick a calm moment, ideally side by side (a walk, a drive).
Name one specific thing: "You've seemed really tired lately." Avoid labels like "depressed".
Ask an open question: "How are things, really?" If they don't want to talk, say "I'm here when you do" and leave it.

routines.title: Side-by-Side Time
routines.description: Do something ordinary together, such as cooking, a walk or an errand. Talking is often easier when it isn't the point.
routines.parentGoal: Stay connected when face-to-face talks feel like too much.
routines.childOutcome: Has easy company, and a chance to talk without pressure.
steps: Suggest something low-key you both don't mind doing.
Let silence be fine; don't steer toward how they're feeling.
If they bring something up, listen first and ask what would help.

routines.title: Offer One Practical Thing
routines.description: Ask what would make this week a little easier, and do one concrete thing they say yes to.
routines.parentGoal: Help in a way that lightens their load without taking over.
routines.childOutcome: Gets real support while staying in charge of their life.
steps: Ask: "Is there one thing I could take off your plate this week?"
Offer examples if they're stuck: a meal, a ride, help with a form or a call.
Do just that one thing, and check later if it helped.

routines.title: Encourage Support, Respect Their Choice
routines.description: If they're struggling, encourage them to talk to a doctor or counselor, and offer to help them find one, while accepting it's their decision.
routines.parentGoal: Make professional help feel normal and easy to reach.
routines.childOutcome: Knows help is available and that you'll back them up, without feeling pushed.
steps: Say why you're raising it: "I care about you, and you've been carrying a lot."
Offer practical help: finding someone, booking, or a ride. Many schools and workplaces offer free counseling.
If they say no, accept it for now, and come back to it gently another time.

routines.title: Know the Warning Signs and Your Plan
routines.description: For you: learn the signs that someone may be in danger, and keep the numbers for getting help right away close at hand.
routines.parentGoal: Be ready to act quickly and calmly if things get serious.
routines.childOutcome: Has a parent who knows what to do if they're ever at risk.
steps: Learn the warning signs: talk of hopelessness or being a burden, giving things away, withdrawing from everyone, or talking about hurting themselves.
Save your local emergency number and a crisis line in your phone (in the US, call or text 988).
If you're worried about their safety, ask directly and get help right away; don't wait.

routines.title: Look After Yourself Too
routines.description: For you: supporting a struggling adult child is hard. Take a few minutes for yourself, and find support of your own.
routines.parentGoal: Stay steady enough to support them over the long run.
routines.childOutcome: Has a parent who stays calm and available, rather than worn out.
steps: Do one small thing that refills you today: a walk, a call with a friend, rest.
Talk to someone you trust about how you're doing, not just about them.
Consider a support group or counselor for parents; you don't have to carry this alone.
